utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to all. May I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted and Tom Hannis for the Prosecution assisted by Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic, Dragan Krgovic, and our Case Manager, Jason Antley. Sorry because I have some problems with computer. It's okay now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would remind the witness. Good morning, sir, I would remind you that you are still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, witness. To save time, I already gave you your statement and the attachment you had before you yesterday. At several points during your evidence yesterday, you mentioned Crisis Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff for Banja Luka municipality was founded in 1991, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the staff, or rather, the national Defence council, if that's what you mean, which grew into the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This body, the National Defence Council, as you call it, included representatives of the SDA party, the HDZ, the SDP, reformists, and the SDS, all the relevant political parties; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And your representative on that body was Mr. Emir Dzanic, right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That National Defence Council was established at that time in keeping with the current law on the basics of All People's Defence and social protection; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please make a pause for the interpreter's between question and answer. That Council for National Defence, as you call it, which was identical in all its features to the Crisis Staffs that appeared later, continued to work in that composition all the way until the end of 1991 or the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't accept that it had the same jurisdiction as a Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that this National Defence Council had grown at one point into a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You withdrew from the National Defence Council, when I say you, I mean the SDA party, towards the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then the SDA party founded its own Crisis Staff in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had exclusively humanitarian --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please answer my question. Did the SDA party form its own Crisis Staff in March 1992, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that staff was headed by Casim -- sorry, Asim Jakirlic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the same time the SDA party stopped working on the Assembly of the municipality of Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before March.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But this termination was not complete, one Emir Busatlic, a member of your SDA party and MP continued to sit on the Banja Luka municipal Assembly; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Also Mr. Gumic and Mr. Kuzmic SDA members, remained on the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this Mr. Gumic, although Bosniak by ethnicity, was Chef de Cabinet or secretary of the municipal secretary Radic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What was his position in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe vice-president of the municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So he was the first assistant to the municipal president?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And he continued in his post from March onwards in 1992 although the Party of Democratic Action walked out of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You gave them orders as to all your membership, I suppose, to stop working on the municipal Assembly of Banja Luka, but they did not obey?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't me who gave them orders. It was the Executive Board. I signed them, but it was the Executive Board who issued the instructions, not me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "Executive Board," you mean the Executive Board of the party in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka then. But you as president of the SDA party and president of the Executive Board signed this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With this Mr. Gumic who was vice-president of the Assembly of Banja Luka, you met several times in the course of 1992 at some official inter-party meetings or municipal meetings or meetings with Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there were no such meetings between us within the party, and I can't recall that at the meetings we had with Mr. Radic he attended. I'm talking about three meetings. I can give you the dates, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I look at my papers where I have these dates?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had one meeting with Mr. Radic on the 24th of June, the 8th of December, 1992, and the 1st of March, 1993 during my tenure in Banja Luka. I believe that Mr. Gumic may have attended the first meeting, but I'm sure he did not attend the other two. However, in my reports you can find precise information because I wrote these reports on the very same day and included the names of those present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until what time, to the best of your knowledge, did Mr. Gumic continue as vice-president of the municipality of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the moment when he decided to leave Banja Luka himself, but I really did not pay attention to that any more. I simply wasn't able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, he was a member of the SDA, obviously he was one of the more prominent members since he was appointed vice-president of the municipality of Banja Luka on behalf of the SDA party, and that's the second highest position in the municipal hierarchy. He continued as an SDA member, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may answer your first question first, he was nominated to that position while there was a sort of vacuum between the election of the SDA party president, to which post I was ultimately appointed officially by secret ballot, and the moment when the president left us. In the meanwhile, we had a temporary body leading the party and unfortunately it was precisely in this vacuum period that some key events happened, and in this vacuum, Mr. Gumic somehow jumped in. I can't understand to this day how because we had many good, educated people. Second, we did not want to expel him from the SDA except in the case of Mr. Busatlic. We gathered signatures and had him excluded from the municipality of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please, our time is limited. I would really appreciate it if you would focus on the question. If I may sum up, and please answer with a yes or no, Mr. Gumic, regardless of the circumstances of his election, was elected vice-president of the Banja Luka municipality as a cadre and representative of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Despite the decision of the SDA party not to participate in the work of the Assembly and contrary to that decision, Mr. Gumic continued as vice-president of the Banja Luka municipality throughout 1992 and later and still remained a member of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that one can then legitimately claim that the SDA party participated in the authorities of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not agree with that because I already told you which decision we had made and it was in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, you have been a member of the SDA party since it was founded?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a regional board of the party for the Bosnian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know people from the SDA party at the regional level?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew most of them, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the regional board?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ex officio I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know the vice-president of the SDA for Kotor Varos, Mr. Cerkic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only very slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He was also a member of the regional board, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, when in the coalition of national parties the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ you won elections in 1990 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't it true that you made an inter-party agreement on the division of positions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but proportionately to our electoral results.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I did not ask you about the provisions of that inter-party agreement. I only want to know if there was one. If there was an agreement on the division of posts?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen that agreement, but one can say it existed. In fact, to be even clearer, we referred to an inter-party agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it the case, Witness, that all three national parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina together stated as their main goal to replace communists or members of the league of communists from all leading positions in all layers of society?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the statute of our party, I never have seen such a statement. It's another matter that there were misgivings they might win elections, and I can say that at the beginning, none of the parties were preoccupied with such issues. We had many more serious matters to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that communists, or the League of Communists, or the communist regime persecuted members of national parties?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They persecuted certain nationalists because at that time there were no national parties, or perhaps you mean the newly-elected national parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of them may have been targeting in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, isn't it logical then, that the moment you got into power by virtue of elections, it was the basic objective of all parties to bring their own people into leading positions and replace the communists?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, I am not among these nationalists who were persecuted and convicted sometimes, and in the party that I led, it was not an objective, a goal. But, of course, we wanted everything done according to the outcome of the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true, however, that it was the purpose of this inter-party agreement on the division of posts, to replace the previous authorities and to place members of your respective parties to all the leading positions in society in keeping with the inter-party agreement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the SDA party is concerned, we nominated our candidates for leading positions from the ranks of people who did belong to political parties, but they also had quite separately certain superlative qualifications and I can give you names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in the local level, I'm interested in the level of the republic. Give me one name of a senior official from the SDA party who had been a communist and remained in his position at the level of the republic. Was there such a person in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, take, for instance, Fikret Abdic. I don't know if Mr. Gumic was part of the previous regime, these were only Bosniaks but look at Croats, Mr. Pejanovic was previously a communist and so on and so forth. If you look at the ambassadors, and that's also a very high position, a great percentage of them used to be communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the executive arm?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that respect as well, many people on the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You talked yesterday about non-Serbs being laid off, and you emphasised physicians; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: P462 was shown to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call it up again, please. I'm interested in Article 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You remember giving your comments on this document from June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you commented on Article 1, paragraphs 1 and 2, and you said that the document referred to non-Serbs, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, paragraph 3 of this same Article 1 applies to employees of Serbian ethnicity, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Article 3 says that these positions enumerated earlier may not be filled by non-Serbs but may not be filled by Serbs either who had not proven their ideological profile and suitability, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is basically about banning opponents from certain political positions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it the same principle that was applied according to your inter-party agreement from 1990 against former communists who had not given up their former ideology?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not the same because there is not a single document or verbal evidence that the SDA party acted in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, just a moment, just a moment. I'm asking you in general terms. I'm not asking about the SDA party nor am I trying to criticise the SDA. Nothing could be further from my mind. I'm talking about all nationalist party or national parties, the SDA, the SDS, the HDZ, and your own inter-party agreement. It stipulated, if you will agree with me, that certain standards be applied to the members of the former authorities, namely that they should be replaced?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a moment. If members of the former authorities remained in that position, then how were you able to place your people in the same positions? Were there two presidents of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm trying to say that as far as the SDA and the HDZ are concerned, to the best of my knowledge, new leading staff, new leading structures were being formed out of people who had certain qualifications and who expressed their loyalty to the SDA. They did not have to be members. And we appointed such people to the municipality of Banja Luka, I can give you names. Mr. Kosulcic [phoen] was a member of the League of Communists, and he was appointed to a municipal position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the SDA was not very popular with intellectuals of the Islamic faith or Muslim Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by who was in the leading positions in our party and our council, I don't think that conclusion is justified. Intellectuals, generally speaking, did not join the newly established political parties in great numbers which is understandable, but I can give you the names of a dozen professors, I believe that's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But for a nation-wide party, it's hardly enough, but I don't want to go into that now. I'll ask you another question, sir. Isn't it true that the SDP, the Social Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a predominantly Muslim or Bosniak party?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the SDP that ran in the democratic elections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the very one.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have relevant information. They have that information in the SDP, but speaking about Banja Luka, yes, that conclusion can be drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When we spoke about that a minute ago, namely that one of your members was on the Municipal Board of Banja Luka, didn't the members of the SDP, mostly Muslims, remain in their positions in the municipal Assembly of Banja Luka and took part in its activities?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you reformulate that question a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, okay. Although I'm trying to keep things short. Is it true that the Social Democratic Party in the Banja Luka municipality in the municipal Assembly which was predominantly Muslim took part in the activities of the municipal Assembly during 1992, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to this document. Yesterday you commented and read an interview with Mr. Brdjanin about a certain Slobodan Cvijetic who was replaced from the position of manager, or director, even though he was a Serb, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that he was replaced because that -- because persons from mixed marriages were also replaced; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Mr. Cvijetic's mother and father are of Serb ethnicity, that he is not the offspring of a mixed marriage?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But his wife is a Croatian woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but his wife being a Croatian woman doesn't mean that he comes from a mixed marriage?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, well that may have been -- I may have misspoken. I want to say that there was a mixed marriage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, my question was the following: You don't want to say that the reason for his replacement was the fact that his wife was a Croatian woman?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of the reasons. It can be seen in the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, isn't it true that this gentleman, although if I may say that a thoroughbred Serb was replaced for ideological reasons and not because his wife was a Croatian woman or for any other reason?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Brdjanin provides the answer to that question in that interview. I believe that answer should be recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we are not examining Mr. Brdjanin here, we are examining you. You gave us your comments to Mr. Brdjanin's interview yesterday, we have that document. Here is what I put to you now. That Mr. Slobodan Cvijetic the director of a successful company in Banja Luka although he was a Serb was replaced for purely ideological reasons, he was an ideological opponent and not for on ethnic grounds. Do you agree with me, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree only partly, because if his wife had been a Serbian woman that would never have happened because he was a recognised expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that if he had divorced his wife he would have remained in a managerial position?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that, or I couldn't claim that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you have just said if his wife were a Serbian woman, obviously you are focusing on the fact that his wife is a Croatian woman?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard from his family that this was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but people will talk, won't they? When you spoke to my learned friend yesterday, you were shown a newspaper article about a group of doctors, specialists from Banja Luka losing their jobs, they were Muslims, Bosniaks, and in September 1992 they were laid off. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I read your statement correctly, which we have in front of us, you went into details explaining that but do say, if you don't remember everything, you mentioned four or five names of esteemed doctors, specialists who were Muslims or Bosniaks who in December 1992 were laid off because they didn't respond to the summons to go to a military hospital near the front line?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that applies to some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 13 of your statement, you mention that the mobilisation or the obligation to serve in the military applied to all three ethnic groups, Muslims, Croats and Serbs equally, and that those who acted in accordance with that order were sent wherever necessary and those who didn't were -- to those who didn't sanctions were applied?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the laws and regulations existing in Yugoslavia in all republics, the duty to serve in the military was seen as a highest duty of any individual?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must correct you. This was within the remit of the highest bodies of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which never issued such a call for mobilisation. It was local authorities that did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we are speaking about December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but Bosnia and Herzegovina existed as a country then, and we were obliged to obey the institutions of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina and not the institutions of individual municipalities where there had been a user patient of power or the authorities of some regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you saying that you don't know that the Republika Srpska had been created in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that Bosnia-Herzegovina was internationally recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we are speaking about facts. It is not for us to interpret them. That's for the Chamber to do later. We are speaking about the facts now. I'm asking you now, since this is about December 1992, you know that the Republika Srpska was in existence, I believe at one moment it was called the Republika Srpska Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that there was a mobilisation order in the Republika Srpska and you lived in the territory of the then Republika Srpska and of present day Republika Srpska; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So that the mobilisation order which was in force in the territory of Republika Srpska applied to all citizens of Republika Srpska irrespective of their ethnicity at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You certainly know that there have been numerous instances when members of the Serbian ethnic group were laid off and they were taken to court for refusing to respond to the mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally do not have such information, but I have heard of such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us comment what you said yesterday. What you -- or rather, let's go to page 53, line 6 and 7. There you commented -- no, you can't find it in your statement, I'm referring to the evidence you gave yesterday. The reference was to the transcript. It's page 53 of yesterday's transcript of your testimony, line 6 and 7. When you commented your meeting with Mr. Radic on the 15th of April 1992, do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which date did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: April 15th, 1992. You were reading a newspaper article about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that's the one I don't have listed here. What was your question again? I apologise again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you gave evidence to the effect that the article from "Glas" was shown to you which dealt with your meeting with Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, I got a bit confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So I would like to ask you once more to pause briefly between my question and your answer for the sake of the interpreters. When you spoke about that yesterday you said that you expressed your concern and then my learned friend asked you whether you went there again, and you replied, Whoever complained risked losing their life, do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was the Prosecutor's question about complaints to the members of the CSB, and that is what my reply referred to. But whoever complained to other institutions too also ran that same risk, so that my answer is affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, you said to us a short while ago you went to see Mr. Radic three more times, 24th of June, the 8th of December, and the 1st of March 1993, and you also had two meetings with General Talic and other military leaders about these same issues. That's not a contentious issue. And we can see that nothing happened to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but we were speaking about individual complaints, so if somebody attacks you in your house and if you complain individually, you risked something bad happening to you. We were the representatives of associations of non-Serbs and in that capacity we were able to have meetings. But individual complaints were practically impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know, sir, but you too are an individual, an individual with property, so that you would have been in the same position as other non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I was in the same position. I believe that you have the information that I went through awful torture, that I lost my property, that those who accompanied me were also imprisoned and so on, so half the people who went to those meetings with me were imprisoned. I think give you their names if you want. Or they were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, a military court in Banja Luka convicted you and those others to long-term prison sentences for espionage. I am not referring to what happened when that group was arrested in 1994, I'm speaking about the period relevant for this case and that is 1992. About this other aspect you will probably speak with my colleague. I'm interested in 1992. As far as I was able to conclude from your statements in 1992, you personally didn't have any major problems, or did you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we disregard the fact that my house was being shot at, then you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, it was war, but so there was shooting in Banja Luka elsewhere, not only at your house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was shooting, but it's different when someone comes to your house and shoots at you, points a gun at your head.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about Kotor Varos yesterday and what was happening there on pages -- on page 58 of yesterday's transcript line 20 up to page 59 line 3. You mentioned people being slaughtered, whipped, tied to trees, et cetera. Were you in Kotor Varos when those things allegedly happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that time, but I spoke to some people while Mr. Zdravko Pejic was with me. And in spite of the terrible situation they confirmed that. I later spoke to witnesses from Vecici and to the parents of the victims, and they all confirmed that beyond any doubt. I also spoke to the HDZ president, what was his name again? Maric. And he also confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So let me conclude, you didn't have any direct knowledge but you got information through intermediaries, by word of mouth?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, in your statements and in your evidence you insist that the SDA of Banja Luka, that is the party which you led, didn't have any weapons in 1992 and that in February you did ask the SDA to supply weapons, but they never arrived; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that in Zagreb too, somebody was telling you about delivering weapons in the territory of Banja Luka and that you asked that person for weapons too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then you were at a meeting at which there was a discussion about weapons that you were to receive from the HVOV Jajce which already had delivered some weapons but you never received any weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I believe that Travnik was also mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "Travnik," you mean the HVO of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You did confirm that you brought automatic rifles from Sarajevo for you and another member of the SDA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that -- one of these automatic rifles you kept to yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that you knew that unauthorised possession of weapons was a crime, especially automatic weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that is why you discarded that weapon in the Vrbas River when you heard that the police would come to search your house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, isn't it true that the actions of collecting illegal weapons who were implemented from 1990 in line with the decision of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina headed by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and on the basis of the order of the minister of the interior Mr. Delimustafic, they are all Muslim Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say because I don't have the necessary information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that there were check-points at all major access roads to towns and that those check-points were in existence in -- or rather throughout former Yugoslavia at that time in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw those check-points in person at the time when travel was still possible. Even when in 1992 I went to Zagreb which we mentioned yesterday, I heard of the existence of check-points on the road to Gradiska, so I went by way of Samac, but I never saw any check-points myself, so I cannot confirm that from my personal experience. Furthermore, when I was in Sarajevo in 1992, which I mentioned in March, I never saw those check-points. I went from the railroad station to my apartment freely and I never saw a check-point. That's really the truth. I cannot confirm that. I don't know the situation in other areas. As far as I know, I can say that probably there were such check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that there was no check-point on the access road to the city of Zagreb in 1990 or 1991 where they asked you for ID, asked you whether you had weapons, searched your car?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody asked me anything. I went by way of Samac and I had no such experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But you knew of a check-point on the road to Gradiska and that's why you chose a different road?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But when I went to see my son in Slavonski Brod in 1991, I went to Slavonski Brod, I don't remember the exact date, on the motorway there was some sort of a check-point manned by soldiers, and I stopped there and described that in my book. But I stopped there because I wanted to of my own accord. Because I saw armed people in the field threatening us, and I stopped to inquire what that was about. We were naive to the extent we had no idea what was going on, which is corroborated by the fact that we were travelling with a child in our car.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's not in dispute and you certainly know that at that time there was a huge amount of illegal weapons around -- supplied from all sides and smuggled and purchased, changing hands?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your book and in your witness statement on page 22, you stated that the leader of the SDA party from Prijedor towards the end of 1991 told you that they had over 2.000 rifles in Prijedor and one small gun, cannon; do you remember that statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand that correctly, that means that in Prijedor in 1991 there were over 2.000 armed fighting men among Bosniak Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't mention another thing, namely that they said it was exaggerated, flamboyance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that the meeting held in Zenica with the Patriotic League where all the regions participated and that was towards the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, isn't it the case that the Military Council of the Patriotic League was surprised by the quantity of weapons that Bosniaks, Muslims, possessed in the Bosnian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about this from a man, not from the council. It's all relative, therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. About this you say everything is relative, whereas yesterday and today you keep telling us that some things were agreed or happening in the territory of a certain other municipality and you only heard about it, but it's true, whereas this other piece of information, you also heard it from someone is relative?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not saying that. I'm just saying that someone told me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that in your book you stated that this Military Council of the Patriotic League estimated the Krajina to be in a much better position than other areas to organise armed resistance and conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I heard from that person, but it was not an official meeting, it was a chat over coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, you are the one who put that information into your book. If you did not believe it to be true, you probably wouldn't write it.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote many things in the book to link up various events. That doesn't mean that I stand behind everything written there. A chat over a cup of coffee is one thing. A document is quite another.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, does that also apply then to your witness statement because you said the same thing in your witness statement and whatever is not documented is not completely reliable. Is that what you are trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe this person was telling me this tendentiously because we did not have a particular relationship of trust. Other information that I got, I often verified and these were people who were either linked to me through the SDA or we had some sort of privatise or they were friends of my associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But you did not check this information, I suppose, because you knew that the commander of the Patriotic League, Mr. Sefer Halilovic in the autumn of 1991 came to Banja Luka to see how the organisation of the Patriotic League was coming along and you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an excellent question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted has an intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, just a moment ago Defence counsel stated that this witness had made the same statement about the Patriotic League in one of his statements. I was hoping that Defence counsel could refer us to where in the statement that is just so we can confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The witness talks about this very piece of his book, or the reference to his book is on page 23 of his statement of 2000, 2001. I will give you the paragraph, it's penultimate paragraph and it's in Serbian version. I'm sorry, I have a Serbian or B/C/S statement. It says on page 18: "I was talking about the meeting that was held in Zenica on which all regions participated so the data on arms can be compared. On that particular meeting, the Military Council of Patriotic League was astonished by the data because they were surprised by the numbers and they estimated that the Bosnian Krajina was in far better position than other regions for organising the rebellion" -- and well, it doesn't say rebellion, it's, I'm sorry, I'm not very good with the translations. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We found the reference, and we would object to the question because the statement continues exactly as the witness says that: "I did not attend this meeting. I learned about it from an individual who is dead now, I have to warn that the above comments should be taken cautiously." So I don't think there was an inconsistent testimony here today about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wasn't suggesting that it was inconsistent testimony, I just said that he wrote that in his book and confirmed it in his statement, the very same thing in -- what he wrote in his book, and the witness gave a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prosecution maintains its objection, because again he doesn't in a sense confirm it, he actually say it is should be taken cautiously, but nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Olmsted, this is a matter for you to which you can return in re-examination. I'm not sure it's a basis for an objection to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday when you were talking about the arming of Serbs you said that the military armed them; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was, in fact, about issuing arms to reservists and members of the Territorial Defence; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if the military is arming its own reservists in the Territorial Defence then by the nature of things it should be in keeping with the law and strict records would be kept as to who was issued with weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but only Serbs got them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's because Bosniaks, Muslims, on the instructions of your party refused to report to military reserve units and mobilisation call-ups?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to finish my answer to the previous question, referring to Sefer Halilovic. Well, please allow me to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, my learned friend from the Prosecution will have a chance after I finish to conduct additional examination, and he will take up all the facts that he believes need clarification. Now, in my turn I'm asking you, isn't it true that Bosniaks would not respond to mobilisation call-ups although it was illegal to refuse?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosniaks received public instructions through the press by the SDA not to respond to mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course not everyone obeyed this proclamation of the SDA and those Bosniaks, Muslims who did respond to the call-up, received weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this issue of weapons again had nothing to do with ethnicity, the only criterion was whether the person responded to the call-up as was his legal obligation or not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mobilisation is one thing, distributing weapons door to door is quite a different thing. That was called receiving weapons, not issuing weapons. When weapons are issued, you are in uniform and you sign a receipt. This was distribution of weapons to civilians of only one ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We discussed this a moment ago, sir, and we agreed that the army was arming it's reservists and members of the Territorial Defence and you agreed that was legal, that records were kept, and that it was in conformity with the law?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one thing --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then you said that it was problematic because only Serbs were involved and then we agreed that Bosniaks, if they had responded to the mobilisation call-up, would have received weapons as well, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as mobilisation is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the fact that somebody receives a weapon while not wearing a uniform at that very moment does not mean he is not receiving -- that he is not a reservist. He signs a receipt that he is receiving a weapon from supplies, but he is a member of the Territorial Defence or the reserve?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the Territorial Defence, and we never received any weapons unless we had been mobilised first and wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You are talking about peacetime?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about a time before this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir, I have no further questions for you. [In English] I'm finished with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Krzic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I am lawyer Pantelic appearing here for Mr. Stojan Zupljanin. Mr. Krzic, you are a tolerant man, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because you were a diplomat and a politician in the past, you are a person of moderate views who is always trying to find a solution through dialogue?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only thank you for that opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You stated in one of your witness statements that your family was in the partisans in the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us a few details about the members of your family who fought in the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four of my paternal uncles were members of the partisan movement, some of them from the very start from 1941 through the end of 1942, and my father worked as an illegal for the partisan movement in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And your family has lived in Banja Luka for several generations, you are an old urban family?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the paternal side, yes. On the maternal side we are not from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And for several generations you have been a prominent family?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I suppose that from your childhood you have been of Muslim faith?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And when you became a member of the League of Communists in 1970, the times were like that, it was necessary to get along in service, et cetera. Why was your mother unhappy?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minor correction that matters to me a great deal however, they came to ask me to join the party after my volunteer work to help the population stricken by the earthquake. My mother was disappointed probably because the entire family, including my aunts on both sides, were members of the communist movement and she was intimately against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is not a very important issue, I can tell you straightaway, but I infer from this that your mother was not really a communist sympathiser?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was a believer, a religious woman. I cannot really make these differences. Religion was respected in my home but it was concealed. In those times, the communist times, it didn't do to display any religious feelings openly. But there was absolute respect between both sides of the family, those who believed and those who didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I quite understand. As a man who lived through some good times because we have to admit, in those times, the times of Tito there were a lot of good things, would you agree that in Bosnia and Herzegovina a balance was always sought between the interests of the three constituent peoples?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As for the expression, the freedom of expression and democratic freedoms and other aspects of democratic society, it was not quite so liberal. It was sort of held tightly with an iron hand?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the approach was restrictive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: However, the national principle was observed in politics, the principle of national parity in proportion, in big companies as well, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, and you will correct me if I'm wrong, in those times one couldn't say that any of the ethnic communities were really oppressed or threatened or pushed out by the majority of other communities?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the main part, yes, although statistics from that period seem to show that in the army and on the police force this principle was really disrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At the expense of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say at the expense of non-Serbs. I don't have the statistics before me, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course, that is your impression. Let's not go into any detail, however --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, we are coming up on the break. It's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it was my impression it was 10.30. So thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness is brought in to court, I would like the record to show that Mr. Cvijetic has joined us now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. While the witness is being brought back to the stand, the Chamber noting that the present schedule anticipates that the witness who is to follow the witness now on the stand, his testimony would be completed tomorrow, and the Prosecution is unable to present a witness for Friday, that Friday's slot would be most usefully spent dealing with a number of procedural matters which both parties have, and therefore, the Court -- the Chamber intends to sit on Friday to deal with these matters and accordingly requests counsel from both sides to have a list of those issues by the close of today's work so that we would know the issues with which we would be concerned come Friday morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krzic, we are about to continue the cross-examination. Even after the multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the principle of equality of peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is the protection of their vital interests was honoured; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were indeed indications to the effect that the previous practice would be continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And a coalition agreement was struck between the HDZ, SDA and the SDS to establish government structures jointly from the highest to the lowest level; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to deal with some very brief issues from the surroundings of Banja Luka, I mean the historical context, but it is clearly linked to this situation. It is a generally known fact that in Croatia during World War II on the border with Bosnia, there was Jasenovac, a notorious concentration camp where several hundred thousand Serbs and numbers of other ethnicities were killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It is also a known fact that in the surroundings of Banja Luka in the hamlet of Drakulici in February 1942 about 2.300 Serbs were killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm numbers generally speaking, but I know of this massacre so I can confirm that it took place, but I must also add that the monument which was erected there during communism mentions the number of 220 people, so I cannot confirm the figure you stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us not go into these details, but what matters to me is that you are familiar with that event and the surroundings of Banja Luka during World War II. Now we are dealing with quite different things. You will also agree that in that period of suffering in the Second World War in the Bosnian Krajina a significant number of Serbs fell victims such as in Sanski Most, Bihac, other places around Banja Luka, et cetera. These are historical facts. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I hold you in high esteem, but you are asking questions to which the answer cannot be ambiguous, but this being a specific situation, I would ask you to take into consideration the victims of other ethnicities at the same time and the same places. I don't want the Chamber to get the impression that crimes were committed only against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course you are entitled to your opinion, I don't want to question that, but I want to ask you whether you know that after the conflict in Croatia broke out in 1991, several tens of thousand Serbs, around 50.000 at that time, fled Croatia and came to Banja Luka in 1991. Did you witness that process?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a process which took some time, it didn't happen at once, but the figures that we spoke about at that time were up to 5.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Krzic, do you personally distinguish citizens and the population of a town from inhabitants of rural areas, that is village folk? Are these all people of the same level?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a person who has the same approach toward everybody, but I must also say that I am aware of the huge differences that exist between rural populace generally speaking of which I was reminded recently, and townsfolk who are custom to co-existence in the same era.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So it is your position, if I understand you correctly, that there are traditional cultural sociological and other differences between urban populations and rural populations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, significant differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You will probably also agree with me when I say that when village folk come to town and rise to some positions of authority, they also jeopardize the positions of townsfolk?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During the war in propaganda and in political speeches, you will probably agree with me there was much exaggeration on all three sides, Muslim, Croat, and Serbian; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And each side at some moments and in line with their intentions used some derogatory expressions for the others; non-Serbs would call Serbs Chetniks; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then Muslims were called Turks or balija; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And Croats were called Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That was a part of public speech and the ways of that time; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, speaking about Banja Luka, I will say, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You as an educated and tolerant man would not use, or did you at that time, use the derogatory term of Chetnik to refer to a Serb?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a private conversation, yes, but never in public. But I must immediately add that I would use the term Chetnik only to refer to killers, people killing others or people who would themselves -- who would present themselves as Chetniks, but not otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But let us return to your book witnessing crime and your love toward Bosnia, you use the term Chetnik or the Serbian Chetnik aggression and the like almost on every page; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe that is compatible with what you and I both said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is to say apart from privately, you also publicly categorised the Serbs in this manner in your book?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as a generally as that because there were also Serbs who couldn't bear all that and who behaved humanely, very humanely. I also stressed that among other information that we received, there was also the term Croatian cadre, although they were not only Serbian, they were also Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Apart from being an intellectual and a diplomat, you are also a writer, so I suppose that in that literary jargon sometimes exaggerations are made; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Krzic, have you read the Islamic declaration whose author is the former president of the SDA, Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read it once, maybe twice. I don't have it. I was looking for it because I wanted to remind myself what it says, but I couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We won't go into details, but as far as you remember, your attitude toward that is positive. You have no objections to what Mr. Izetbegovic wrote there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my opinion is that writing that should not be a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But I'm referring to the views put forward in the Islamic declaration, you share those views?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very poorly, but there were some very general views put forward there that go beyond Bosnia and being a practical man to me that declaration had no practical value whatsoever for Bosnia-Herzegovina or for the Bosniak people at the time. I take that to be more of a philosophical work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes philosophical works have serious value. One of the views put forward there is that there is no co-existence between Islam and other religions, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it exists, I disagree with that. I never agreed with that. You can't find anything of the kind in my biography.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with the part of that book that deals with the uppermost duty of a Muslim to build a Muslim state, create Muslim institutions, and be a majority there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are asking me about the declaration. Why don't you simply put something to me and ask me whether I agree with that? Because I only took a superficial look at that declaration. I had many more important things to deal with, such as the book "Islam Between the West and the East."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But do you agree with that view?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I absolutely disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When the SDA was established, I understand the word "action" from its name as something stemming from the Islamic declaration, which means that Muslims must fight continuously to reach some positions. This action presupposes offensive, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I must -- before answering, I must add something. The author of that name was the well-known musician Safet Isovic who was a leftist, possibly not really a communist, but anyway, action can be interpreted as work. As a young man I took part in labour actions, that's what they were called at the time, actions. That's part of a jargon, a socialist jargon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me then, Mr. Krzic, now that we are speaking about this, did the programme of the SDA include the ideas of Bosnia-Herzegovina being a secular state without very strong ties with religious institutions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to go ever into the phrasing of your question, but yes, I believe that was so and on general terms that there should be no official ties between the state and the religion, so, yes, religion was respected but certainly Bosnia-Herzegovina was not to be a religious state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But let me ask you another thing. What does Mahsuz Sellam mean, the greeting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sellam means greeting, and Mahsuz means special greeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, let me spell that correctly. [In English] Expression of M-a-h-s-u-z then another word, S-e-l-l-a-m. [Interpretation] Now, were there any Serbs in the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you speaking about Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I noticed in several letters you wrote that in the communication between you as the president of the SDA of Banja Luka and headquarters and also in the communication between you as a man who collected information and who was at the BiH mission in New York that you often finish your letters with the greeting Mahsuz Sellam; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As opposed, but it's really just an assumption, correct me if I'm wrong, that the members of the SDA who are of Serbian or Croatian origin, that is Christians, wouldn't feel comfortable when confronted with this basically religious greeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in the BiH mission, which should have had staff from all three ethnicities, isn't it quite unusual to use a religious greeting in diplomacy?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't a diplomat at the time, I was the leader of a, well, provincial party, I can say at the time. That greeting was used as a sign not of difference, but more of an expression of protest. Nowadays, that phrase is mostly used in private letters, not only today, it's been like that for awhile. In Sarajevo at least, I can see that the greeting Ciao is used widely. That's an Italian greeting. It's probably been chosen so as not to make that difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now that you've mentioned Sarajevo and bearing in mind that you have a house in Banja Luka, which is your property, do you also own an apartment in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have property in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You got an apartment from the government institutions; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I bought the apartment when it was privatised, and I sold a house in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To who did that apartment in Sarajevo belong before you bought it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't like provide an answer to that question, you can do so, but if necessary, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the second apartment of a person and as they had two apartments, one of them had to be vacated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was that person of Serbian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I paused because of the transcript. Mr. Krzic, you are a smart man, an intellectual. I'm sure you will agree with me when I say that these unfortunate events in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina had as a consequence massive migrations so that nowadays a negligible percentage of Serbs lives in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we compare it to the previous number, I certainly suppose that the number is significantly smaller, although I don't have any exact figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Likewise there are hardly any Serbs in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking there have been movements of population --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We have been far around during the first stage of your cross-examination. I'm bewildered as it to where we are going, so I think you should tighten up and get to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I take your instructions, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But let us finish this. We will agree that rather a large or huge number of Serbs came to the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you acknowledge the reality that the Republika Srpska is in existence and that it's a constituent entity of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that the bodies -- the authority of the bodies of the Republika Srpska is also defined by this international agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You will certainly agree with me when I say that during the war between 1992 and 1995 a large number of camps was to be found in territories controlled by Muslim forces where Serbs were imprisoned and a certain number of Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have never seen them. I've heard of them, but I don't have the information that you have mentioned. But certainly I will agree that people were imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As far as Banja Luka is concerned, I believe that you mentioned yesterday in answering to my learned friend's question, that there was an SDA initiative to establish new municipalities in Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only the SDA, I mentioned that it was the initiative of all parties except the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the objective was, and you have described it in your book too, that based on the survey of the justification to establish these municipalities, the former territory of Banja Luka be divided into some six municipalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But the objective of that initiative, and I will now mention these envisaged municipalities, namely Stari Grad, Novi Grad, Budzak, Bronzani Majdan, Krupa na Vrbasu, and Ivanjska?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I made a mistake yesterday, I believe I mentioned Stricici, but that may have been wrong, you understand that I cannot remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you are saying that it was actually an initiative by your party to establish municipalities with a non-Serb majority, that's what it says in your book, you mentioned that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, I would have to take a look at it, and you would have to provide me with a reference to a page in my book, but generally speaking no municipality apart from one possibly, no municipality could have had a Bosniak majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Your statement reads that you were one of the founders of the SDA in Banja Luka, and in September 1991, what was your position in the SDA of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I was secretary, then I became president.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was vice-president of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And of course you took part in all discussions in the party and in all decision-making. We'll now look at a document originating from your party branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask for 1D1. Now we also see the B/C/S version as well as the English one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The copy is not too good but I'd like to draw your attention -- first of all, you are familiar with the document, it comes from the Municipal Board based in the cultural hall, you see the SDA stamped at the bottom? And finally, you mention this initiative in your book. It's an SDA document; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been, but I don't remember this document. I still haven't had time to look at it properly. I'm looking at the English version because the B/C/S one is bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Of B/C/S version, please, of second paragraph. Second paragraph of B/C/S version just enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me help you, if I can. It says that the Banja Luka municipality is one of the largest in Yugoslavia, and you discussed this with my colleague yesterday. It was not very efficient and there were certain initiatives to divide it up. What's important to me in this document, which reflects the initiative for all this, is that the main motivation, as it says in the last sentence, is "in this environment, Muslims have an advantage over the Serbian element, 38 to 36 per cent, while together with other ethnic groups, they comprise a two-thirds majority, 64 per cent." Can you see this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your party initiative to set up these municipalities was, in fact, driven by the SDA's idea to create municipalities with the majority non-Serb population, that's what we see from this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are mostly right, but I don't agree with the non-Serb population part. I don't how authentic this document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, let's be quite clear. The motivation of this move was to create municipalities where Muslims together with other ethnic communities would have an approximately 64 per cent majority?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are reading the last sentence. You are taking it out of context. You have to look at this passage in its full context.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, how do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are also economic considerations, and as the political situation was as it was, non-Serbs could hardly wait to get a chance to have some influence on local self-government, and this was a real chance and if we had had real authorities, we would have maintained peace. There would have been no such conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you again that my position is this, the SDA wanted to create several municipalities in Banja Luka with a majority non-Serb population in order to be able to form a government and to exercise power efficiently. Just answer me with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now we look at another document, 1D4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a draft of the statutory decision of the organisation of a Stari Grad Banja Luka Municipal Assembly in the process of being established. Are you familiar with this document, Mr. Krzic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say I am because I don't have it. I haven't seen it before. At least I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Krzic. We got these documents from the Prosecution, but that concerns our procedure, not you. Was there any discussion at your party meetings about the draft of this decision to organise the Stari Grad Banja Luka municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can't remember participating in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to ask you about something else now. One of the objectives of your work in Banja Luka in a large percentage of your secret clandestine activities that you mentioned in the book was to lobby to get the deployment of international military forces in Banja Luka, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were our wishes. We didn't have any other objective except to report the real situation in the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. SFOR finally came so your wishes came true. Let's move on. Was it one of your objectives to draw media attention to Banja Luka and Bosnian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was it another of your objectives in your clandestine work to form a professional team to monitor the situation in Bosnian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You call that a team, I call it a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Let it be a group. Was it the case?
